notebook:
PLAN: First make a C4/C5 split, inspect sharpness and costs, then build high-value C5+ product branches and a compact light-end branch; optimize settings using cached solves. Step 1: feed split.
Feed contains $3.36B/yr total product value. Highest priorities: n-pentane, C6 paraffins, 2-methylpentane, n-octane, heptane, cyclohexane. Avoid indiscriminate tiny-product separation in expensive scenario. Initial root targets C4- tops and C5+ bottoms at moderate pressure.

note: Establish a blend-oriented full sequence with sharper splits, especially the difficult C6 paraffin/naphthene boundary.
notebook:
PLAN: Build a seven-column blend-focused sequence: root C5-/C6+, lights to C3 and C4 blends, heavy split to C6 paraffin/naphthene blends and pure C7/C8/C9; then tune costly/impure columns and prune low-value branches. Step 2: establish revenue baseline.
Root at 60/3/3 was broad and cost $206M/yr. Full product value ~$3.36B/yr. Blends avoid difficult isomer purification. C6 paraffin/naphthene cut is the hard N-hexane/MCP boundary, so use 100 stages and RR8. Skip ethane recovery (only ~$4M/yr). Other agent's low-reflux direct sequence produced no sellable streams, confirming sharper cuts are needed.

note: Sharpen all blend boundaries and add ethane rejection so the C3 stream can qualify; this should establish substantial revenue before cost tuning.
notebook:
PLAN: Build an eight-column blend sequence: root C5-/C6+; lights to ethane rejection, C3, C4, C5 blends; heavies to C6 paraffin and naphthene blends plus C7/C8/C9. Step 3: make every cut sharp enough to earn revenue, then reduce costs/prune weak branches.
Low reflux gave zero revenue. Blend values are approximately C3 $71M, C4 $186M, C5 $618M, C6 paraffin $1.44B, naphthene $396M, C7 $332M, C8 $359M, C9 $104M per year; ethane is negligible. The prior TT top needs an ethane-rejection column before C3 can qualify. Root and C5/C6-paraffin boundaries are the key difficult splits. Current trial raises all separation ratios substantially.

note: Prune to the two most valuable heavy blends and move the B cut from within C6 to C6/C7 by increasing boil-up.
notebook:
PLAN: Focus first on the very valuable C6 paraffin and naphthene blends using three sharp columns (C5-/C6+, C6/C7+, paraffin/naphthene). Once profitable, add C5 and lighter blends only if their revenue exceeds cost.
The old nine-column design earned only $163M against $1.31B cost. Root 90/10/10 cut near C5/C6 but leaked ~142 mol/s C5 into B. B 60/4/4 incorrectly cut within C6; increasing boil-up should move the cut to C6/C7. BT then needs a higher top fraction to take all four paraffins overhead and both naphthenes below. Prune all other branches for this decisive test. Blend values: C6 paraffin ~$1.44B/yr, naphthene ~$396M/yr, C5 ~$618M/yr.

note: Restore a known-convergent root and move all three cuts toward their component-flow targets with higher boil-up, especially the paraffin/naphthene split.
notebook:
PLAN: Establish a converged three-column C6 recovery train (C5-/C6+, C6/C7+, paraffin/naphthene), then tune splits using component flows and only add lighter recovery if profitable.
Root 90/10/12 failed; R185 shows 50/4/6 converges but leaves heavy C5 leakage. Increase root boil-up toward 10 while retaining its convergent structure. R185 B 70/6/5 puts only 853 overhead versus desired roughly 1536, so raise B boil-up. Its BT 120/10/8 cuts within paraffins (370 tops), so BT needs much more boil-up to put all four paraffins overhead. Target products: C6 paraffins about $1.44B/yr and naphthenes about $396M/yr; three columns can plausibly cost under this.

note: Establish the full blend sequence with a clean root cut and higher C6 paraffin recovery, while adding the valuable C5 blend and light blends.
notebook:
PLAN: Build a five-column blend train: clean C5-/C6+ root, C4/C5 and C3/C4 light splits, then C6/C7+ and paraffin/naphthene splits. Tune cuts to component-flow targets, then reduce cost.
Root 50/4/6 gives a nearly clean 1507 mol/s light tops, unlike boil-up 10 which leaks ~300 C6 overhead. Use R233's B 70/8/9 for a full C6 cut, but its BT boil-up 14 splits within paraffins; raise to 20 to bring n-hexane overhead. Add T at boil-up 12 to push residual C4 out of C5, and TT for C3/C4. Maximum blend revenues are roughly C3 $60M, C4 $175M, C5 $610M, C6 paraffin $1.15B/yr.

note: Move the C6 split to the paraffin/naphthene boundary so the large tops stream qualifies as the valuable C6-paraffin blend, while cutting its excessive size and reflux cost.
notebook:
PLAN: First make the existing five-column train profitable by recovering a sellable C6-paraffin blend, then prune/tune low-value branches and reduce column cost.
Root 50/4/6 gives clean 1507 mol/s C5- tops. T 60/8/12 plus TT 50/5/5 currently sells C5 ($566M) and C4 ($157M). B 70/8/9 makes a 995 mol/s C6-rich tops. The BT split at 120/12/20 wrongly cuts between 2-methylpentane and heavier paraffins, leaving both products unsold. Raise boil-up to the 30 maximum and reduce stages/reflux to 80/8: this should carry 3-methylpentane and n-hexane overhead while retaining naphthenes/C7+ in bottoms, at much lower cost. BTT was 90% paraffin and BTB 88%; moving the cut toward n-hexane/methylcyclopentane is the key value step. Do not add an ethane column for only ~$73M C3 revenue until the main blends are profitable.

note: Combine the best C4 settings with the proven cheaper T column and a moderately leaner root to reduce the dominant cost while preserving both blend cuts.
notebook:
PLAN: Build from R418's profitable three-column C5/C4 core, cut root/T costs without losing blends, then test C3 recovery only if cheap.
R418 scores +0.379 ($737M revenue, $571M cost); TT boil-up 4 improves C4. R417 shows T=50/7/12 retains both blends and saves $14M. My B/BT branches are uneconomic. Now combine R418 with T trim and root 40/3.5/6; root dominates cost ($306M), so its trim has largest upside. Preserve dp=0.1 and TT=50/5/4.

note: Restore blend purity by keeping root reflux at 4, while testing a modest five-stage root reduction and the proven cheaper T column.
notebook:
PLAN: Restore the profitable three-column C5/C4 core, trim root and T costs without losing either blend, then consider only high-value incremental recovery.
My 40/3.5 root failed both blends: excess DMB entered T and C5 fell to 92%; T's shorter 50 stages alone was not the problem. R470 proves 50/4/6 root + 50/5/4 TT gives $727M revenue. Now test root 45/4/6 (retain separation-driving reflux/boil-up) with R417's T=50/7/12. Avoid C3 branch: its maximum ~$73M cannot justify another column. Heavy branches were uneconomic.

note: Test a substantially lower root pressure on the best core; this targets the dominant $306M root cost while retaining the proven cuts and downstream settings.
notebook:
PLAN: Restore the profitable three-column C5/C4 core, trim root and T costs without losing either blend, then consider only high-value incremental recovery.
Best core is R518: root 50/4/6, T 50/7/12, TT 50/5/4, reward .383. Root stages below 50 slightly reduce revenue without meaningful cost saving; T boil-up 10 destroys C5. Root dominates cost at $306M and all columns still use only 10% pressure drop. Test root dp=.5 first while retaining downstream settings: lower pressure should improve relative volatility and reduce diameter/duty costs, though condenser temperature may fall. Keep TT high pressure to avoid light-end refrigeration. Avoid C3 and heavy branches: prior attempts uneconomic.

note: Restore R518 and test a modest reflux reduction only in the C4/C5 splitter; its C5 blend has a few percent purity slack, so this may cut energy cost without losing revenue.
notebook:
PLAN: Restore the profitable three-column C5/C4 core, trim root and T costs without losing either blend, then consider only high-value incremental recovery.
Best core is R518: root 50/4/6, T 50/7/12, TT 50/5/4, reward .383. Root dp=.5 destroys both cuts and is much costlier; root double effect also fails to preserve the split. Root stages below 50 slightly reduce revenue without meaningful saving; T boil-up 10 destroys C5. Root reflux 3.5 failed convergence. Now test only T reflux 6.5: C5 currently has ~99% blend purity, so there is limited but plausible slack, and lower reflux should reduce its $197M cost. Keep root and TT fixed. Avoid C3 and heavy branches: prior attempts uneconomic.

note: Restore the best core and lower only the C4/C5 splitter reflux; its C4 product has substantial purity slack, so this may save energy without sacrificing either blend.
notebook:
PLAN: Restore R518, then reduce TT energy using its large C4 purity margin; retain both valuable blends and avoid previously uneconomic branches.
Best core R518: root 50/4/6, T 50/7/12, TT 50/5/4, reward .383. T reflux 6.5 loses C4; root dp changes, double effect, and root stage reductions do not help. R616 root boil-up 5.7 cuts cost but loses $21M revenue, net worse. TTB is currently 100% C4 and TTT is unsold, so lowering TT reflux is the most promising cheap test. Try TT reflux 4.0 while holding its boil-up at 4.0. Avoid heavy and C3 branches.

note: Combine the two best independently validated cost reductions: root boil-up 5.9 and a 40-stage T column, retaining the proven TT settings.
notebook:

Best shown core R663: root 50/4/5.9, T 50/7/12, TT 50/5/4, reward .386. R664 shows T at 40 stages remains qualified and saves about $1.3M; root 5.9 saves about $2.6M with modest revenue loss. These changes should be roughly additive. TT reflux 4 is worse; heavy and C3 branches are uneconomic. Avoid root 5.7, pressure changes, double effect, and extra columns.
